opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think this question gets to one of the core motivations behind Nested Learning.

Right now the dominant paradigm is that you pre-train a huge model once, freeze it, and then whenever the world changes or you want new capabilities, you either fine-tune the whole thing or retrain. That's expensive, and it's also brittle, because when you update all the parameters on new data you risk catastrophic forgetting. So you pay a lot of compute and you still might lose what the model already knew.

Nested Learning looks at it differently. We view a model not as one monolithic set of weights trained by one optimizer, but as a system of nested optimization problems, each with its own context flow and its own update frequency. Some components update very frequently, almost at the level of each token, like attention or fast-weight memories. Others update more slowly, and some change very rarely and hold the more persistent, abstract knowledge. You can think of it as a spectrum of memories, which is what we call a continuum memory system, rather than the strict short-term versus long-term split we have today.

The computational benefit comes from that frequency structure. You don't need to touch everything every time new information arrives. The fast levels absorb new context cheaply and locally. Only what proves useful over longer horizons gets consolidated into slower levels, and those updates are sparse and infrequent. That's loosely inspired by the brain: consolidation happens at different timescales instead of rewriting the whole cortex every time you learn something.

So instead of periodic, very costly full retraining, you move toward continual learning where most adaptation happens in components that are cheap to update, and the expensive parameters change rarely. That also helps with forgetting, because knowledge stored at slower levels is protected from noisy short-term updates.

I want to be honest that this is still early. Our experiments, including the Hope architecture, are at research scale, and there are real engineering questions about doing this efficiently on today's hardware, which is optimized for big dense, synchronous updates. But conceptually, I think separating learning by timescale is a much more sustainable way to keep models current than retraining from scratch every few months.

r001.rationale: The response says, “You don't need to touch everything every time new information arrives,” and describes fast components updating frequently while slower components update rarely, communicating that updates are limited to a subset of parameters at each step.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that the cost of keeping a model updated today comes almost entirely from the fact that we treat the whole network as one monolithic thing with a single update clock. Everything gets touched on every step, or nothing does. So you either pay for full fine-tuning or retraining, or you freeze the model and bolt on retrieval and hope that covers the gap.

Nested Learning starts from a different picture. A model is not one optimization problem, it is a nest of optimization problems, each with its own context, its own memory, and its own update frequency. The attention layer is a very fast inner loop that updates its state on every token. The weights that gradient descent writes into update much more slowly. The optimizer state, things like momentum, sits in between. Once you see it that way, the question of "how do I keep this updated" stops being a single question and becomes "which level actually needs to change for this piece of information."

That reframing is where the cost savings come from. Most of what a model encounters day to day does not require rewriting slow parameters. It belongs in the fast levels, in what we would call the continuum of memory, where the model has components that update at different timescales and the information naturally lands at the level whose timescale matches it. A fact that matters for the next thousand tokens goes in a fast memory. A pattern that keeps recurring over many sessions gradually consolidates into slower levels. You only pay for a gradient update at the deep, expensive layers when something actually persists long enough to justify it. Compare that to today, where every update either happens everywhere or nowhere.

The architecture we built around this, the HOPE model, is really a demonstration of that idea. It has a self-modifying component that can learn its own update rule, and it couples that with a multi-level memory, with each level running at a different frequency. The nice thing is that the expensive operations get amortized. The slow components are updated rarely, so their cost is spread over many tokens. The fast ones update often but they are small. That is a very different cost profile from "run backprop through the entire network again."

I also want to be honest that this does not make updating free. It changes what you pay for. You are trading a periodic, enormous retraining bill for a continuous, much smaller one, and the engineering challenge shifts to deciding how information moves between levels. But I think that is the right trade. Biological systems do not retrain the whole brain to learn what happened this morning, they have a hierarchy of consolidation. Nested Learning is an attempt to give models that same structure, so that staying current becomes an ongoing property of the system rather than an event you have to budget for.

r001.rationale: The response says different components update at different frequencies: the fast components update each token, while slow weights update much less often, and the fast components are small. This communicates restricting each step’s updates to a small part of the model.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that keeping a model updated shouldn’t require updating every part of it at the same frequency. Some information changes very quickly, while other knowledge is useful over much longer periods. If we treat all of that as one optimization problem, we end up spending a lot of computation updating things that may not need to change.

With Nested Learning, we can think about the model as a set of interacting learning processes operating at different timescales. Faster processes can incorporate new information, while slower processes preserve more stable knowledge. That gives us a way to allocate computation according to what actually needs to adapt, rather than repeatedly retraining the entire system.

It doesn’t make the cost disappear. You still have to decide what gets updated, how frequently, and how information moves between those processes. But it changes the question from ‘How do we retrain this large model every time something changes?’ to ‘What part of the system needs to learn from this change?’ That’s where I see the opportunity for greater efficiency.

r001.rationale: The response says different parts update at different frequencies and asks which part needs to learn, but it does not clearly state that each time step updates only a small subset of model parameters.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that you don’t want to update everything at the same frequency. Some information changes very quickly, while other knowledge should remain stable for a long time. In Nested Learning, we think about those as different learning processes operating at different timescales.

That gives you a way to allocate computation more selectively. A faster memory can absorb new information without requiring a full update of all the model’s parameters. Then, on a slower timescale, you can consolidate what’s useful into more persistent knowledge.

Of course, that doesn’t make the computational cost disappear. You still pay for learning and for maintaining those memories. But it changes the question from, “How often do we retrain this entire model?” to, “Which part needs to learn this information, and how often should it update?” That’s where I see the opportunity for keeping models current more efficiently.

r001.rationale: The response says computation can be allocated selectively and that a faster memory can learn without updating all parameters, but it does not state that each time step updates only a small subset of parameters.
